guides.title: England from ice-age landscapes to 1900
guides.description: Early people, Roman towns, port cities, industry and reform across England.
guides.intro: England’s earliest record begins with footprints in Norfolk and worked flint in Suffolk. Much later, the archive includes boat planks near Dover, Roman road remains, medieval land surveys and factory disputes. These sources measure different things and make different lives visible. Follow several of them across the map to see how movement, labour and authority changed between the Pleistocene and 1900.
guides.scope: Selected histories in the area now called England, with cross-border connections wherever the record allows. The mapped places represent discoveries, built sites or documented events.

map.scope: Approximate discovery sites, built places and historical reference localities on a modern basemap.

points.description: Timber buildings, tools and discarded goods from Coppergate preserve a record of craft production and trade.

points.description: The charter addressed demands involving taxation, liberty and the relationship between royal and baronial authority.

points.label: Fountains Abbey, North Yorkshire
points.description: Religious property passed to the Crown as Henry VIII’s government closed monastic houses across England and Wales.

points.description: A cast-iron arch was assembled above a river corridor already important for making and moving goods.

points.description: A large reform meeting at St Peter’s Field called for parliamentary change. Armed forces entered the crowd and killed and injured participants.

paragraphs.text: The tracks at Happisburgh and the bones at Boxgrove belong to different Pleistocene landscapes. The long gaps between them are part of the archaeological record. At Star Carr, waterlogged lake-edge deposits preserve evidence of more recent hunter-gatherers. Later still, pegged wooden walkways in the Somerset Levels show how farming communities engineered routes across wet ground.

sections.heading: Coastal travel, town streets and Rome

paragraphs.text: The Dover boat documents Bronze Age woodworking and seafaring. Roman ditches at Richborough belong to a later invasion and supply system. Roads linked ports, forts and civilian towns. At Wroxeter, a military site developed into an urban settlement with its own public buildings and households. The separate Hadrian’s Wall guide traces the frontier at the scale of forts, crossings and neighbouring settlements.

sections.heading: North Sea contacts and medieval power

paragraphs.text: The Sutton Hoo burial joined local power to a wider world of ships and traded or gifted objects. Lindisfarne drew people and books across the North Sea and Irish Sea, while York’s excavated workshops show the ordinary trade and craft of a later urban community. After 1066 a new ruling elite used tools such as the Domesday survey to record land and its resources.

sections.heading: Land, representation and the royal state

paragraphs.text: The Runnymede agreement and later parliamentary summons grew from conflicts over how kings should govern. Surviving documents usually speak in the voices of people who could call assemblies, grant charters or order surveys. Tudor records of the dissolution also expose transfers of property that changed work, welfare and land use around former monasteries.

sections.heading: Industry, Atlantic trade and urban protest

paragraphs.text: The Severn’s ironworks and the Liverpool–Manchester railway moved goods through expanding industrial districts. Liverpool investment also enabled forced Atlantic transportation, as the Brookes voyage record documents. In the new industrial towns people organised over public representation and conditions at work. The records of Peterloo and the Bow matchworkers show different tools of protest and collective action.

For London, the nineteenth-century census comparisons count nearly 2.81 million people in 1861 and 4.23 million in 1891 within the administrative county used by the retrospective table. Its geographic scope differs from the broader metropolitan area. The exhibition in Hyde Park gives another view of the city during this period, as a place where imperial and industrial goods were staged for a mass public.

guides.title: Wales from the first people to 1900
guides.description: Cave archaeology, maritime exchange, Welsh polities, language, coal and slate.
guides.intro: Cave burials, copper workings and forts form part of the record of Wales, alongside books, contested marches and industrial landscapes. Some connections ran along the Welsh coast, some crossed to Ireland, and others followed river valleys into the borderlands. The map connects selected places across those different settings.
guides.scope: Places in modern Wales and the Welsh borderlands, from the Middle Pleistocene to the onset of the Penrhyn dispute in 1900. Early regional labels follow the relevant archaeological or documentary evidence.

map.scope: Approximate discovery sites, built places and historical reference localities on a modern basemap.

points.description: Blaenavon’s furnaces and worker housing formed part of a rapid expansion of heavy industry.

paragraphs.text: The teeth and stone artefacts from Pontnewydd predate the deeply coloured burial at Paviland by a vast interval. Gower’s cliffs and the Great Orme’s caves now frame modern coasts. At different points in the Ice Age, people approached these places through very different environments. Dates from the caves describe separate episodes and surviving people.

sections.heading: Farming communities and the work of metals

paragraphs.text: The mound at Bryn Celli Ddu reused the site of an older enclosure. The Great Orme mine shows miners following and working ore veins in a different part of the landscape. At Castell Henllys the postholes of houses anchor reconstructions of community life. Some of the most elaborate regional Iron Age objects, including parts of vehicles and weapons, survived near a former Anglesey lake.

Caerleon and Segontium preserve different scales of Rome’s military presence. Later, an earthwork associated with Mercian king Offa crossed parts of the borderlands. Near Llantysilio the rulers of Powys used a carved Latin inscription on Eliseg’s Pillar to recall dynastic ties. The earthwork and the inscription tell different stories about power across a shifting frontier.

sections.heading: Conquest, diplomacy and Welsh in print

paragraphs.text: Medieval church networks centred on places such as St Davids. Edward I’s castle and walled town at Caernarfon changed access to land and commerce after conquest. Glyndŵr later used diplomatic correspondence to pursue a different status for Wales and its church. Tudor legislation reorganised secular administration, while William Morgan’s 1588 Bible supported widespread use of written Welsh in worship.

Furnaces, coalfields, canals and tramroads connected south Wales to markets far from the valleys. The Merthyr and Newport risings and rural toll protests arose from different pressures and forms of organisation. In the northwest, quarry workers’ dispute at Penrhyn began in 1900. Working sites, settlements and transport routes explain how industrial output depended on everyday lives.

guides.title: Scotland and its islands through 1900
guides.description: Mainland and island histories from hunter-gatherers to medieval polities, mills, crofting and rail.
guides.intro: From struck flint in South Lanarkshire to the steel spans of the Forth Bridge, surviving places record very different ways of moving, living and governing. Scotland’s mainland and islands connect to each other and to Ireland, Scandinavia and wider Atlantic routes. Those connections have their own timelines.
guides.scope: Mainland Scotland, the Hebrides, Orkney and Shetland through 1900. Separate landscape guides cover selected island and mainland monuments in greater depth.

paragraphs.text: South Lanarkshire’s late-glacial flint scatter resembles tools found elsewhere in northern Europe, giving archaeologists a basis for assessing its age. Mesolithic hearths and hazelnut shells at Cramond can be placed more closely in time. Offshore and coastal sediments preserve changes in sea level and the Storegga tsunami, helping explain why some early coastal settings are difficult to find or recognise today.

Stone houses in Orkney preserve hearths, rooms and furniture. Uprights at Calanais in Lewis and the surviving tower at Mousa in Shetland belong to other landscapes and activities separated by long periods of time. The linked island guides show how these buildings fit among smaller remains, farms and routes by sea.

Roman military movement left roads and fortifications, including the Antonine line and the corridor near Trimontium. Later, Dunadd organised craft, exchange and royal authority in Argyll, while religious communities at Iona and Portmahomack developed different ties around the Irish Sea and North Sea. These networks can be traced through excavation, objects and historical records.

sections.heading: Norse settlements, Scottish kingdoms and unions

paragraphs.text: Norse households at Jarlshof and the cathedral at Kirkwall are evidence for northern island histories. The pledges and annexation of Orkney and Shetland between 1468 and 1472 changed their relationship to the Scottish Crown. Mainland struggles over sovereignty produced events and documents such as Bannockburn and the Arbroath letter. Parliamentary union with England followed in 1707, a century after the union of crowns.

Culloden and its aftermath changed some patterns of authority in the Highlands. Later estate decisions brought displacement in places such as Sutherland. Crofters drew on local organisation to press for protections. In the industrial regions the mills at New Lanark, the growing population of Glasgow and the Forth railway crossing illustrate different effects of demands for labour and transport.

guides.title: Ireland from early settlement to 1900
guides.description: An island-wide guide to prehistoric settlement, medieval Ireland, plantation, famine and land reform.
guides.intro: The history on this map belongs to the whole island of Ireland. A marked bear bone, passage graves, harbour excavations, letters from exiles and census tables offer distinct views of life on the island. Sites in the north connect to the separate Ulster guide, which follows movements across present-day jurisdictions and the North Channel.
guides.scope: Selected evidence from across Ireland through 1900, including north–south and overseas connections. Modern jurisdictions locate sources and sites.

sections.heading: What can a cave bone show?

paragraphs.text: A reindeer bone from Castlepook has a reported cut mark and an age of about 33,000 years. This possible evidence predates the better-established cut marks on a bear bone from County Clare. The surviving finds are sparse and record individual actions. Later, work at Mount Sandel and Hermitage reveals early postglacial evidence of housing, food processing and burial.

The wall lines below peat at Céide Fields, passage tombs in Meath and the Giant’s Ring near Belfast preserve different uses of land. How much of the field network at Céide belongs to the earliest farming phase remains under discussion. Copper workings at Ross Island and settlement evidence on Inis Mór widen the record to places of resource extraction and habitation.

Tara acquired great significance in traditions of Irish kingship. Clonmacnoise grew at a strategic water and land crossing, and Nendrum’s tide mill shows the scale of a monastery’s engineering and food processing. The Gospel book associated with Kells and Iona followed a religious network, while excavations in Dublin and written accounts about Waterford document different routes by sea.

The strongholds at Trim, Carrickfergus and Donegal grew from distinct forms of lordship. Ulster leaders went into exile in 1607, and Crown-backed plantations recast holdings in the early seventeenth century. Campaigns around the Boyne and uprisings such as those in 1798 followed other struggles over rule. Union with Great Britain took effect in 1801.

The Dublin–Kingstown railway began operating in 1834, a decade before potato blight deepened widespread hardship. Relief records document a part of the catastrophe, and passengers such as those on the Jeanie Johnston connect it to North American ports. Campaigns over land continued into the later century. In Dublin, repeated censuses describe the borough’s changing population within one published historical comparison area.

guides.title: Ulster and the north of Ireland through 1900

guides.intro: The Bann, the Foyle, Lough Erne and Strangford Lough carried people and materials through the north of Ireland. Ports along the North Channel reached out to Scotland, while medieval and early modern centres were part of histories that also include Donegal. Use the points to explore these connections and the growth of industrial Belfast.

points.date: Later sixteenth and early seventeenth centuries
points.description: The castle became a seat of the MacDonnells, whose relationships and political interests crossed the North Channel.

points.label: Rathmullan area, County Donegal
points.description: Hugh O’Neill, Rory O’Donnell, Cúchonnacht Maguire and followers embarked for continental Europe.

points.label: Derry/Londonderry
points.description: A circuit of walls was built around the plantation city under the auspices of London companies.

points.label: Jennymount Mill, Belfast
points.description: A mill complex developed near the waterfront as linen manufacturers expanded production.

points.label: Queen’s Island shipyard district, Belfast
points.description: A nineteenth-century shipbuilding firm enlarged its operations on Queen’s Island.

points.label: Belfast city census area
points.description: The census returned 255,950 people for its City of Belfast tabulation.

paragraphs.text: Hut plans and pits at Mount Sandel reveal early postglacial work and settlement above the Bann. The broad bank at Ballynahatty preserves a Neolithic monument beside related but differently dated features. At Beaghmore, peat kept multiple stone settings and cairns visible to archaeologists, even where individual dates are hard to determine.

sections.heading: Timber structures, precious metal and mills

paragraphs.text: The circular timber structure at Navan Fort is one stage in a long-used landscape. The gold miniature boat deposited near the Roe offers an unusual record of ancient water travel and skill, through the decisions of a craftsperson. Early medieval communities placed working infrastructure beside navigable water, as the mill on Mahee Island and the monastic buildings on Devenish demonstrate.

The strongholds at Carrickfergus, Donegal and Dunluce belonged to overlapping histories of Anglo-Norman expansion, Gaelic lordship and cross-channel kinship. The Flight of the Earls and the construction of a fortified plantation town on the Foyle mark different parts of the shift to more direct Crown rule and large-scale changes in landholding.

sections.heading: Textile work, shipbuilding and urban life

paragraphs.text: Belfast’s linen works and shipyards gathered workers and capital near the harbour. At Jennymount, expansions preserve evidence of a mill’s changing needs. The shipyards occupied a different part of the waterfront and developed on a different scale. The 1891 census counts 255,950 people within the city scope used in its table, a date-specific measure of an industrial city.

guides.title: Early people and changing landscapes of Britain and Ireland
guides.description: Footprints, cave remains and hearths from intermittent Pleistocene activity to postglacial settlement.
guides.intro: One coastal find records footsteps in ancient mud. Another is a set of teeth. Others are marks on bones, hearth debris and worked stone. The map brings these discoveries together to show where and when archaeologists can place early activity in Britain and Ireland, across a record with long breaks.
guides.scope: Selected early hominin and postglacial evidence across Britain and Ireland. Dates before written history come from geological dating, radiocarbon measurements and comparison of objects. Rounded ages retain their uncertainty on the timeline.

map.scope: Approximate discovery sites, built places and historical reference localities on a modern basemap.

points.label: Happisburgh coast, Norfolk
points.description: A footprint surface records several people walking across estuarine mud on a landscape now on the Norfolk coast.

points.label: Pakefield coast, Suffolk
points.description: Sharp flakes and a flint core are evidence of human activity in a warm Pleistocene landscape.

points.label: Boxgrove area, West Sussex
points.description: A lower leg bone and two teeth accompany an archaeological record of activity near an ancient shoreline.

points.label: Barnfield Pit, Swanscombe
points.description: Three pieces of the same skull were recovered at different times in river-terrace deposits at Swanscombe.

points.label: Pontnewydd Cave area, Denbighshire
points.description: Teeth and stone artefacts recovered in the Elwy valley provide early evidence of human activity in what is now Wales.

points.label: Goat’s Hole, Gower
points.description: The remains of a young man were found with red ochre and worked objects in a cave above the Gower coast.

points.label: Castlepook Cave area, County Cork
points.description: A reindeer bone from the Castlepook cave assemblage has a mark interpreted by zooarchaeologist Ruth Carden as the result of stone-tool butchery.

points.label: Gough’s Cave, Cheddar
points.description: Bones, stone tools and worked antler preserve evidence of activity as people returned to Britain late in the Ice Age.

points.label: Howburn Farm area, South Lanarkshire
points.description: Flint points and other artefacts indicate activity by hunter-gatherers in southern Scotland towards the end of the last Ice Age.

points.label: Great Orme, Llandudno
points.description: Human remains from the cave preserve a late-glacial funerary record and some of Britain’s earliest recovered human DNA.

points.label: Creswell Crags
points.description: A dated layer of mineral growth over an engraving places people’s image-making in the Late Upper Palaeolithic.

points.label: Edenvale cave area, County Clare
points.description: Cut marks on a bear kneecap from the Alice and Gwendoline cave assemblage provide dated evidence of a late-glacial human presence in Ireland.

points.label: Star Carr, Vale of Pickering
points.description: A Mesolithic site on a former lakeshore preserved timber, animal bone, tools and worked antler in waterlogged deposits.

points.label: Cramond, Edinburgh
points.description: Hearths, flint and charred hazelnut shells document visits to a landscape beside the River Almond and Firth of Forth.

points.label: Mount Sandel, Coleraine
points.description: Circular patterns of postholes and pits mark Mesolithic occupation above the River Bann.

points.label: Hermitage area, County Limerick
points.description: A pit contained cremated bone and a ground stone axe at a riverside Mesolithic burial site.

paragraphs.text: Footprints at Happisburgh carry a geological age range of about one million to 780,000 years ago. Pakefield and Boxgrove preserve evidence of other periods. At Boxgrove, bone and teeth give researchers a different way to ask about human ancestry than flint alone. The Welsh teeth at Pontnewydd document an early Neanderthal presence substantially later in the Middle Pleistocene.

sections.heading: Burials and the reach of sparse finds

paragraphs.text: At Paviland the age of the ochre burial comes from the human remains themselves. In Ireland, the Castlepook claim depends on interpretation of a mark on a reindeer bone from a historic collection. Bone from an Irish bear gives stronger late-glacial evidence of human activity through microscopic study and radiocarbon dating. Neither Irish cave by itself records the length of anyone’s stay.

sections.heading: Different paths back as climate shifted

paragraphs.text: Human remains at Gough’s Cave and Kendrick’s Cave have yielded genetic evidence for people with different ancestry affinities, within a small and unevenly preserved sample. At Howburn, similarities in the shape and working of stone tools matter more to dating than a layer sealed by later deposits. Flowstone above a carving at Creswell confines the age of the image from the other direction, giving a minimum age for the engraving.

sections.heading: Water, camps and burial after deglaciation

paragraphs.text: Wet ground preserved timber around Star Carr, while charred hazelnut shells helped date activity at Cramond. Pits and postholes at Mount Sandel anchor an early chronological sequence in the north of Ireland. The cremation at Hermitage reveals evidence of funerary practice. Sediments from the Storegga tsunami record part of the changing coastal geography, with the effects on individual settlements difficult to establish.
